title: Born in Mozambique, Raised in Rajkot: Dolly Vadalia Gets Indian Passport After 26 Years
excerpt: A missed consular birth registration left her without citizenship proof despite a lifetime in India. A Home Ministry memorandum, after MP intervention and verification in Mozambique, has ended the case.
body:
• Dolly Vadalia, born in Mozambique to Indian parents and raised in Rajkot from three weeks old, received an Indian passport on November 11 after a Union Home Ministry memorandum recognised her as an Indian citizen.
  • Her case turned on one missed step: her birth was never registered at an Indian consulate within one year, which Section 4(1)(b) of the Citizenship Act requires for citizenship by descent — an Aadhaar card was not enough to substitute for it.
  • Three passport applications were rejected in 2023 and 2025, and the Gujarat High Court dismissed her petition in April before two Lok Sabha MPs, verification by the Indian mission in Mozambique, and the Home Ministry memorandum resolved the case.
  • For Indian parents whose children are born abroad, the practical lesson is direct: register the birth at an Indian consulate within one year to secure the child's citizenship by descent.

Dolly Vadalia has lived in India since she was less than a month old. She was schooled in Rajkot, took a master's degree from Saurashtra University, married there in 2023 — and until last week, she could not get an Indian passport. On November 11 she finally received one, after a Union Home Ministry memorandum recognised her as an Indian citizen, news agency PTI reported, citing her brother-in-law Ronak Vadalia.

A birth registered in the wrong place

Vadalia was born on February 18, 2000, in Xai-Xai, Mozambique, to Indian citizen parents who both held valid Indian passports, according to the Gujarat High Court's record of her case. Her birth was registered with the Mozambican authorities and a birth certificate issued. What did not happen — in the middle of a flood emergency that forced the family to return to India on March 14, 2000, when she was about 18 to 25 days old, travelling on an emergency certificate — was registration of the birth at an Indian consulate.

"Prachchhak dismissed her petition, holding that she was neither an Indian citizen by birth nor by descent under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act, as Live Law's report of the order records."

That omission controlled everything that followed. Under Section 4(1)(b) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, a child born outside India claims citizenship by descent only if the birth is registered at an Indian consulate within one year, or later with the Central Government's approval. Passport authorities asked Vadalia for consular registration of her birth, cancellation of her emergency certificate, or other proof of citizenship. Mozambique's High Commission told her there is no procedure for cancelling the emergency certificate and that she is not a citizen of Mozambique, the court record states — she had never acquired Mozambican citizenship and never held a foreign passport. She was, in effect, documented everywhere except the one registry that mattered.

Rejections, then a court loss

Two of her passport applications, dated September 29, 2023 and March 24, 2025, were closed on the same ground, the High Court noted; PTI reported three applications in 2023 and 2025 were rejected in total. The issue became urgent after her marriage on July 30, 2023 to Khilankumar Vadalia, a Rajkot resident working in Canada on a work permit — without a passport, she could not join him, and the couple remained separated.

On April 30 this year, a single-judge bench of the Gujarat High Court under Justice Hemant M. Prachchhak dismissed her petition, holding that she was neither an Indian citizen by birth nor by descent under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act, as Live Law's report of the order records. The court left one door open: she could apply for citizenship before the concerned authority, which would decide in accordance with law.

The route that worked

The case then moved through political and administrative channels rather than the courts. Lok Sabha MPs Ramesh Dhaduk and Parshottam Rupala took it up with the Rajkot collectorate, the Gandhinagar secretariat, the Ministry of External Affairs and the Ministry of Home Affairs, Ronak Vadalia told PTI. The external affairs ministry sought the home ministry's opinion; in October last year, the home ministry had reiterated the one-year consular registration requirement and that an Aadhaar card alone could not establish eligibility. This time, after verification by the Indian mission in Mozambique, the Home Ministry issued the memorandum recognising her as an Indian citizen, and the passport followed on November 11.

The lesson for diaspora parents

Vadalia's 26 years of paperwork reduce to a single administrative step that Indian families living abroad control at the very start of a child's life. A child born overseas to an Indian parent is not automatically documented as an Indian citizen for passport purposes: the birth must be registered at an Indian consulate within one year to establish citizenship by descent under Section 4(1)(b). Families who miss that window can find, as Vadalia did, that school records, a degree, an Aadhaar card and a lifetime of residence in India do not substitute for it — and that the eventual remedy runs through ministries and discretionary approval rather than entitlement.
